title: St Brigid (1 February)
hookLine: Irish families weave rush crosses for the spring

lines: OVER THE DOOR FOR THE YEAR.
cards: A bundle of green rushes lies on a kitchen table, still damp from the ditch.

Someone folds one stalk over another, turns the bundle, folds again, and slowly a small square appears in the middle with four arms reaching out. Tie the ends with thread: a cross that looks a little like a pinwheel.
In Ireland, families make these at the start of February and hang them over the door or in the kitchen, and last year's comes down. Not carved: woven from whatever grows by the field.
Behind the custom is a woman, a sickbed, and a story about explaining the faith with what was lying on the floor.

teach.h: A WOMAN OF KILDARE, KNOWN BY TRADITION.
teach.b: Tradition honors Brigid of Kildare as one of Ireland's patron saints. What's told about her comes from lives of the saint written after her time; the Bible doesn't mention her.
The stories show a woman who led a community at Kildare and gave things away, sometimes alarmingly: one has her handing her father's sword to a poor man so he could sell it for food.

teach.h: A CROSS WOVEN AT A SICKBED.
teach.b: The cross comes from another story. Tradition says Brigid was called to the bedside of a dying chieftain who did not share her faith. He was restless and couldn't be calmed.
The floor was strewn with rushes, the way floors were then, so she sat down, picked some up, and wove a cross while she talked about the man who died on one.
The story says he grew quiet, listened, and asked to be baptized before he died.

teach.h: MADE FROM WHAT WAS ON THE FLOOR.
teach.b: That's Brigid's faith in the stories: practical, made from whatever was at hand. Not gold, not marble. Rushes.
Her day falls at the hinge of the Irish year, when the worst of winter is turning and the first lambs come.
Some readers note that the turn of spring was marked in Ireland before Christianity too, and that Brigid's day gathered up that older season.
So the cross over the door carries two hopes: her faith, and the light coming back.
The Song of Solomon puts the second one this way: "For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; The flowers appear on the earth."

how: In Ireland, families and schools weave Brigid's crosses from rushes or straw around her feast day, often hanging the new cross by the door or in the kitchen and taking down last year's.

o: leave and send for a priest to explain things properly.
pick up rushes from the floor and weave a cross while you talk.
games.why: tradition says she wove a cross from the rushes on the floor while she told him about Christ, and he asked to be baptized.

practice: Make a simple cross from whatever is near: two pencils and a rubber band, two twigs, two straws. It doesn't need to be beautiful; Brigid's came from the floor.
As your hands work slowly, think of one thing you're waiting on to turn, the way winter turns, and if you pray, hold it before God as you finish.

wordCard.voice: St Brigid. A saint of Kildare, remembered in tradition for generous hands and a cross woven from rushes at a dying man's bed.
